title: A Terminal Protocol for Program Status (OSC 7501), Mitchell Hashimoto
why_it_matters: It's a generic escape sequence that lets any program tell its host it's idle, working, blocked (with a kind such as permission, question, or auth), done, or errored, with an optional app, id, progress, title, and message. done and error persist after the process exits, while working and blocked don't. Claude Code added support on Oct 8, so terminals that implement it can show working, waiting on you, or done. For a harness this is the cheapest possible 'agent inbox' signal: it works across agents that share no protocol, and it separates the different reasons for being blocked instead of collapsing them into one 'needs attention' badge.
credibility_note: The spec is by Ghostty's author and written product-neutral, and a major agent shipped support within two days. It's still a proposal with few terminal implementations so far.
theme: Attention is becoming infrastructure: "waiting on you" is turning into a terminal-level protocol, gates are failing closed, and fleet supervision is moving to pinned queues and phones, but the evidence says awareness isn't control unless there's a cheap path back to the implementation.

title: ParallelPilot: Supporting Coordination and Monitoring in Parallel AI Coding (arXiv 2609.33113)
why_it_matters: A formative study (N=14) produced PILOT, five supervisory practices: Planning, Isolating, Logging, Observing, and Triaging parallel sessions. The probe pairs a planning interface, a run logger, and an ambient dashboard. In a counterbalanced within-subjects study (N=16), ticket throughput rose 63% on short tasks, people supervised about one more agent at peak, and tracking effort and context switching dropped, with 14 of 16 preferring it. Perceived control and perceived success at redirecting agents did not improve significantly. The authors conclude that high-level awareness needs low-cost paths back to the implementation evidence.
